title: How to Design Your First Platformer Level on iPad
summary: Design your first platformer level on iPad: plan one jump, build reusable ground, match collisions, add a goal and a restart, then playtest it in hyperPad.
body_markdown:
Your first platformer level should teach one movement skill, give the player a safe place to try it, and end before the idea becomes repetitive. This guide shows how to lay out one hyperPad Scene with ground, a jump, a collectible, a goal and a restart, then playtest it. The examples use the Platformer Starter Kit from[Creating Your First Game on iPad](https://www.hyperpad.com/blog/creating-your-first-game-on-ipad) , but the same steps work with any assets.


Build the layout with Objects before adding enemies, coins or final art.


## Plan the level on paper


Define:


- the player’s start;
- one safe movement test;
- one gap or obstacle;
- one collectible or optional route;
- the goal;
- the failure and restart path.


Keep the first level short enough to play several times while editing.


## The level structure


Section Purpose Test


Start area Introduce movement safely The player can move before facing danger


First challenge Teach one jump or timing decision Failure is understandable


Practice area Repeat the skill with a small variation The level does not introduce another system too soon


Goal Show clear completion The player recognizes the ending


## 1. Create or open the Scene


Use one[Scene](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/scenes) . Add a simple background, then place a placeholder Object where the player will start so you can judge scale. You'll swap it for a controllable player later.


A background should help separate platforms, hazards, and UI. Avoid detail that reduces the contrast around interactive Objects.


## 2. Build the ground from reusable pieces


Add one ground Object with the correct collision shape. Duplicate it to extend the floor rather than creating a different Object for every tile.


Use the editor’s grid and alignment controls to keep repeated pieces level.


## 3. Match collisions to the artwork


The collision shape should describe where the player appears to stand. A large invisible edge or a gap between visible tiles can make movement feel inconsistent.


Once you have a controllable player, run the Scene and approach each edge slowly. Watch where the player begins to fall or stops moving.


## 4. Build one jump


Create a gap or raised platform sized for a normal jump. When you test it with your player, try ordinary, imperfect input as well as a perfect jump.


A first level should allow room for early and late input. Difficulty can increase after the player understands the movement.


## 5. Place an optional collectible


Add one collectible where it encourages the player to try the intended route. Use an[Object Tag](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/object-tags) if the same logic will apply to several collectibles later.


A[Collision Event](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/collision-event) can trigger score, sound, animation, and removal. Prevent the same Object from scoring more than once. To build this out with coins and a score, follow[Part 5: Adding coins and points](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/part-5-adding-coins-and-points) .


## 6. Define the goal


Use a visible exit, marker, or end area. When the player reaches it, stop the active challenge and show completion feedback.


The end should not depend on an invisible position the player cannot predict.


## 7. Add failure and restart


Decide what happens when the player falls. The Project might return the player to a checkpoint or reset the Scene.


Test restart several times. Player position, collectibles, score, hazards, camera, and completion state should follow the rules you defined.


## 8. Test the camera and UI


Keep the player, next landing area, and important hazards visible. Make sure score, health, or touch controls do not cover the route.


Test on the intended device orientation and screen size.


## 9. Run a focused playtest


Ask another person to play without instructions. Record:


- where they stop;
- which Object they miss;
- whether the first jump is readable;
- whether they recognize the goal;
- whether restart is clear.


Change one layout problem and test again.


## Next steps


To add a character you control with a joystick, with animation and jumping, follow[Part 4: Creating your player](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/part-4-creating-your-player) in the hyperPad documentation. The full six-part platformer series is listed in[Creating Your First Game on iPad](https://www.hyperpad.com/blog/creating-your-first-game-on-ipad) . Then come back to the tests above and adjust the layout until another player can finish and restart without coaching.
